subject: physics_2
question_text: Explain Doppler effect in light. Distinguish between red shift and blue shift.

mark_split.label: What the Doppler effect in light is

verification.note: The 2+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked: for relative speed v much smaller than c, Δλ/λ = v/c; on approach the observed wavelength decreases (blue shift, λ′ < λ) and on recession it increases (red shift, λ′ > λ); frequency shifts the opposite way to wavelength in each case. The book writes the formulas with the source speed Vₛ and does not state the v ≪ c condition — the condition is added here because the first-order formula is only valid under it.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.
insider_note: Keep the pairing straight — approach means blue shift, moving apart means red shift; one swapped pair loses both distinguishing marks.

steps.label: What the Doppler effect in light is
steps.mark_note: Apparent change in frequency and wavelength
lines: When a light source and an observer move
relative to each other, the frequency and
the wavelength of the light, as measured by
the observer, differ from the emitted values.
This apparent change in the frequency or
wavelength of light is called the Doppler
For a relative speed v much smaller than c,
the size of the wavelength shift is
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Say APPARENT change, say it is measured by the observer, and give the shift formula with its condition v ≪ c.
steps.why: The source emits the same light throughout — what changes is what the observer measures, which is why the word apparent matters. The formula Δλ = (v/c)λ is the first-order result and holds only when the relative speed is much smaller than c.
common_mistakes: Saying the source starts emitting a different wavelength. The emission is unchanged; the observed values shift.
Writing Δλ = (v/c)λ without the condition v ≪ c. At speeds near c the full relativistic formula is needed.
Saying the speed of light changes. The speed stays c; frequency and wavelength shift together so that their product stays c.

recall.must_convey: That relative motion between source and observer makes the observed frequency and wavelength differ from the emitted values, with shift Δλ = (v/c)λ for v much smaller than c.
accept: apparent change in frequency and wavelength
source and observer move relative to each other
delta lambda is v by c times lambda
reject: spectral lines move toward the blue end

steps.memory_tip: One formula, two signs: Δλ = (v/c)λ, minus on approach, plus on recession.

steps.label: Blue shift
lines: Blue shift: when the source and the observer
approach each other, the observed frequency
The spectral lines move toward the blue end
steps.margin_note: One mark. Approach → frequency up, wavelength down, lines toward blue. Give all three.
steps.why: On approach, successive wave crests are emitted from closer and closer positions, so they arrive more often: frequency rises and wavelength falls. Blue is the short-wavelength end, so the lines move toward blue.
common_mistakes: Writing that the frequency and the wavelength both increase. They move in opposite directions; their product must stay c.
Pairing approach with red shift. Approach compresses the waves — that is the blue shift.

recall.must_convey: That when source and observer approach, frequency increases, wavelength decreases, and the spectral lines move toward the blue end.
accept: lines move to the blue end

steps.memory_tip: Coming closer compresses the waves — shorter wavelength is the blue side.

steps.label: Red shift
lines: Red shift: when the source and the observer
move away from each other, the observed
increases. The spectral lines move toward
the red end of the spectrum.

lines.text: Approach: blue shift · recede: red shift

steps.margin_note: One mark. Recession → frequency down, wavelength up, lines toward red — the mirror of the blue-shift line.
steps.why: On recession, successive crests are emitted from farther and farther positions, so they arrive less often: frequency falls and wavelength rises. Red is the long-wavelength end. Light from distant galaxies shows this red shift, which is the evidence that they move away from us.
common_mistakes: Writing the same sign for both shifts. Recession gives +Δλ, approach gives −Δλ.
Saying red shift means the light turns red. The whole spectrum shifts toward longer wavelengths; each line moves toward the red end.

recall.must_convey: That when source and observer move apart, frequency decreases, wavelength increases, and the spectral lines move toward the red end.
accept: wavelength increases when they move apart
lines move to the red end

steps.memory_tip: Moving apart stretches the waves — longer wavelength is the red side.
